parsed.summary: The four theorems state Karp-style NP-hardness of promise problems. Every NP language (defined by a poly-time verifier with polynomially bounded certificates) has a polynomial-time map sending members to YES instances and non-members to NO instances. The problems are: GapCVP with integer target and gap n^{1/400} (ℓ2); binary nearest codeword and binary syndrome decoding with gap n^{1/200}; and ℓp GapCVP for rational p ≥ 1 with gap n^{1/(200p)}. The definitions match the paper's Theorem 1 and Corollary 15 closely. The main caveats are minor. The disjointness fields of the promise problems are `sorry`'d. The ℓp variant admits rational targets, and the ℓp statement itself is not in the excerpt.

glossary.plain: L ∈ NP: there exist a polynomial bound and a poly-time TM2 verifier V with L(x) ↔ ∃ c, |c| ≤ poly(|x|) ∧ V(x,c)=true
Every NP language reduces to the promise problem via a poly-time map with completeness (L(x) → YES(f x)) and soundness (¬L(x) → NO(f x))
glossary.standard_concept: NP-hardness of a promise problem under deterministic poly-time many-one reductions

glossary.plain: YES: bits encode (n, B∈Z^{n×n}, t, r) with n>0, det B≠0, r>0, t∈Z^n and ∃v∈Z^n, ‖Bv−t‖₂² ≤ r². NO: the same shape, and ∀v, (n^{1/400} r)² < ‖Bv−t‖₂²
glossary.note: The lattice is spanned by the columns of B. Squaring is harmless because r>0. Disjointness is sorry'd.

glossary.plain: YES: generator G∈F2^{n×k}, target u, radius R>0, n>0, ∃c with wt(u−Gc) ≤ R. NO: ∀c, n^{1/200}·R < wt(u−Gc)
glossary.standard_concept: Gap nearest codeword over F2 with gap n^{1/200}
glossary.note: The code is spanned by the columns of G (the transpose of the paper's row convention); this is harmless.

glossary.plain: YES: H∈F2^{m×n}, b, R≥0, n>0, ∃x with Hx=b and wt(x) ≤ R. NO: R>0, Hx=b is consistent, and every solution has wt(x) > n^{1/200}·R
glossary.standard_concept: Gap syndrome decoding with gap n^{1/200}
glossary.note: NO additionally requires the system to be consistent. The paper's d_H = min over an empty set would treat inconsistent systems as NO. The Lean NO set is smaller, so the theorem is stronger.

glossary.plain: ℓp GapCVP for rational p≥1: YES ∃v, ‖t−Bv‖_p ≤ r. NO ∀v, n^{1/(200p)}·r < ‖t−Bv‖_p. Instances are well-formed with a rational target.
glossary.standard_concept: GapCVP in fixed finite ℓp norm
glossary.note: There is no integer-target restriction, unlike the ℓ2 version. The exact paper statement is not in the excerpt.
The base is nonnegative and p≥1, so rpow has no junk behaviour here.

lean_claims.plain: GapCVP with integer target, nonsingular integer basis, rational r>0 and gap n^{1/400} (ℓ2) is NP-hard under deterministic poly-time many-one reductions.
Binary nearest codeword with gap n^{1/200} (n = block length, R>0) is NP-hard.
Binary syndrome decoding with gap n^{1/200} is NP-hard. NO instances must be consistent systems with R>0.
For every rational p≥1, ℓp GapCVP with gap n^{1/(200p)} is NP-hard.

paper_claims.plain: A deterministic poly-time map from 3SAT to (B nonsingular in Z^{n×n}, t∈Z^n, r∈Q>0) with SAT ⇒ dist2 ≤ r and UNSAT ⇒ dist2 > n^{1/400} r; hence GapCVP_{n^{1/400}} is NP-hard.
Binary nearest codeword and binary syndrome decoding are NP-hard to approximate within n^{1/200}.

coverage.why: The same promise problem and the same hardness notion.
The same gap and the same definition up to the generator transpose convention.
NO instances must additionally be consistent.
The paper statement is not in the excerpt; the gap n^{1/(200p)} and the rational-p restriction cannot be checked.

flags.explanation: The disjointness fields of all four promise problems are `sorry`'d. They appear true: the gap factor is ≥1 for n≥1, and the length-prefixed encoding with leading dimension looks injective. Still, they are unproved obligations inside the definitions.
flags.probe_idea: Prove `Function.Injective encodeInstance`, and the analogous injectivity for the code encodings, then derive disjointness.

flags.explanation: NO requires the system Hx=b to be consistent and R>0. In the paper an inconsistent system has infinite distance, so it counts as NO. Lean's NO set is smaller, so soundness is harder and the theorem is stronger.

The ℓp statement is not in the excerpt, so its gap exponent 1/(200p) and the rational-p restriction cannot be checked. Its instances also omit the integer-target restriction used in the ℓ2 version, which slightly enlarges the YES and NO sets.
